turns.prompt_text: I've noticed that a good part of problem solving is about giving up Once I put enough action and effort and energy into something giving up entirely as important to get a fresh start Then if so happens if it comes back to me I can start from the very beginning where the thought and originated and I can run through that path again knowing which ones are dead ends
turns.response_html:
There is a massive difference between "quitting" out of frustration and the strategic, intentional act of giving up a path to clear your cognitive stack.

When you focus intensely on a complex problem, your brain naturally builds a hyper-specific mental model of the solution space. The trap is that once a mental model is formed, confirmation bias and functional fixedness lock you into it. You keep trying to force the square peg through the round hole because your brain is heavily invested in the "energy" you’ve already spent (the sunk cost fallacy of problem-solving).

By consciously choosing to drop it entirely, you force a hard reset.

Here is what is actually happening mechanically when you let it go and come back to it:

  • Pruning the Search Tree: When you start fresh, you don't actually forget everything; your brain holds onto the high-level map. You intuitively know where the dead ends are, allowing you to bypass them entirely without wasting active working memory on them.
  • Incubation Period: While your conscious mind is "giving up," your diffuse mode of thinking (the background processing) keeps chewing on the structural elements of the problem without the constraints of your initial, flawed assumptions.
  • Re-indexing from First Principles: Starting back at the "origin thought" allows you to verify if the foundation was even correct. Half the time, the reason a problem becomes unsolvable is that an incorrect assumption was made in step one, and every subsequent action was building on an unstable foundation.

Giving up the attempt is often the only way to save the objective. It's not a defeat; it's a garbage collection routine for your brain.

Do you find this reset happens naturally after a specific amount of time away, or do you have to actively force yourself to wipe the whiteboard clean to get that fresh start?

turns.prompt_text: So one problem of the sunk cost is that In order to keep trying again and starting over, there's some amount of entropy that happens and so it becomes difficult to start over. So I think what I'm trying to say is that every shot counts
turns.response_html:
That makes total sense. Every "restart" isn't free—it carries a real energetic and emotional cost.

When you abandon a path and try to reboot, you aren't just magically teleporting back to the starting line with a clean slate. You are carrying the exhaustion of the failed attempt, and the environment itself might now be messier (more "entropy") because of the half-finished code, the scattered materials, or the mental fatigue.

If you view your energy as a finite battery, you quickly realize you don't have infinite restarts. Every shot does count, which makes the decision of when to pivot or rebuild incredibly heavy.

To manage that friction and lower the "cost" of starting over, it helps to look at how we transition between those shots. Here is a way to think about managing that entropy so a reset doesn't feel like a mountain to climb:

1. The "Clean Up Before You Walk Away" Rule

The hardest part of starting over is often the physical or digital mess left behind by the last attempt. If you walk away mid-struggle and leave a chaotic workspace, returning to it feels exhausting.

  • The Fix: Before you "give up" for the day or the week, spend five minutes putting things back to baseline. Commit your messy progress to a temporary git branch, put the physical tools back on the rack, or wipe down the margins of the whiteboard. Treat the "shutdown sequence" as the first step of your next clean shot.

2. Leaving Breadcrumbs (The "Warm Start")

Starting from absolute scratch is intimidating because of the cold-start problem. If you have to spend an hour just remembering where the starting line was, you've wasted valuable energy.

  • The Fix: When you decide to drop a path, write a single, brutally honest "tombstone note" to your future self.

"I tried X, Y, and Z. X failed because of [Reason]. Y is a dead end because [Reason]. Start next time by looking at the assumptions behind [Core Constraint]." This lets you immediately bypass the dead ends without having to re-experience the trial and error that led to them.

3. Sizing the "Shots"

If starting over feels too heavy, the scope of your "shot" might be too large. If a reset means rebuilding an entire system from scratch, the entropy will paralyze you.

  • The Fix: Shrink the boundaries of what you are throwing away. Instead of scrapping the whole project, can you just "give up" on a specific subsystem or a single design assumption? Isolating the failure means you only have to reset a small sandbox, leaving the rest of your momentum intact.

Every shot absolutely counts, which is exactly why preserving your starting stamina is a skill in itself.

When you feel that friction of "man, starting this over is going to take so much work," is it usually because of the mental drag of re-engaging with the logic, or is it the physical/setup drag of actually resetting the environment to a clean state?
